cards.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation sent a memorandum on Monday ordering local agencies to remove license plate readers from state highways within 30 days. The order came after Governor Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology out of control last week.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the removal decision makes Martin County citizens fundamentally less safe. Budensiek pointed to several major arrests made with the help of the cameras, including the arrest of President Donald Trump's would-be assassin, a kidnapper with two young girls headed to Nebraska, and a traveling rooftop burglary crew. "We stopped and arrested President (Donald) Trump's would-be assassin. Last year, we stopped a kidnapper with two of our young girls headed to Nebraska. We stopped a traveling rooftop burglary crew," Budensiek said.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised license plate readers like Flock cameras after they aided in a homicide arrest last month. "We got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system," Flowers said. Port St. Lucie police is pausing the use of license plate readers in the city, and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office will be limiting license plate reader use to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered persons. Budensiek proposed limiting camera use to criminal investigations and missing persons cases, requiring a case number and report for public record.

cards.teaser: The Florida Department of Transportation ordered local agencies to remove license plate readers from state highways within 30 days after Governor Ron DeSantis called the technology out of control.

hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office discovered a body in the mangroves on Hutchinson Island on Tuesday that investigators believe belongs to Michael Anthony Debevec II, an Oklahoma visitor who was reported missing after last being seen at Chastain Beach on August 26. Sheriff John Budensiek said the clothing on the heavily decomposed body matches what Debevec wore in surveillance video.

Debevec's family filed a missing person's report on Saturday after a good Samaritan found his wallet on the beach near the House of Refuge. The Martin County Sheriff's Office searched the area of Hutchinson Island by land, sea and air. Deputies discovered Debevec's car parked at Chastain Beach and later found his backpack hanging high in a tree about half a mile south of where the body was located.

"They found his backpack hanging high in a tree half an hour or so south of us. As they continued to go through the thick, thick mangroves and brushed sea grapes and mangroves behind us, they located, unfortunately, a deceased body," Budensiek said. The body was found just north of the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island.

Debevec's family said he had gone missing before and had a history of substance abuse, but said he had gotten clean. The Medical Examiner's Office is working to determine the exact cause of death, looking for signs of trauma and performing a toxicology report. Investigators are waiting for a positive identification.

A body discovered in the mangroves on Hutchinson Island is believed to belong to Michael Anthony Debevec II, an Oklahoma visitor who was reported missing days earlier after last being seen at Chastain Beach. The Martin County Sheriff's Office is investigating the body found just north of the House of Refuge, and investigators are waiting for a positive identification. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said he believes the body belongs to Debevec because the clothing matches what Debevec was last seen wearing in surveillance video. The body was found heavily decomposed.

Debevec's family filed a missing person's report on Saturday after a good Samaritan found his wallet on the beach near the House of Refuge. Deputies later discovered Debevec's car parked at Chastain Beach. The Martin County Sheriff's Office searched the area of Hutchinson Island by land, sea and air through Tuesday morning. Deputies found Debevec's backpack hanging high in a tree half an hour or so south of the House of Refuge and continued through the thick mangroves and sea grapes before locating the body.

Debevec's family says he has gone missing before and has a history of substance abuse, but says he had gotten clean. The Medical Examiner's Office is working to determine the exact cause of death, looking for signs of trauma and performing a toxicology report.

hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police paused use of license plate readers Tuesday and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office limited use to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered persons, one day after the Florida Department of Transportation ordered local agencies to remove the devices from state highways within 30 days. FDOT sent the memorandum Monday after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology out of control last week.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Tuesday the state removal decision makes Martin County citizens fundamentally less safe. Budensiek pointed to several major arrests made with the help of the cameras, including stopping President Donald Trump's would-be assassin, stopping a kidnapper with two young girls headed to Nebraska last year, and stopping a traveling rooftop burglary crew. Budensiek proposed limiting camera use to criminal investigations and missing persons cases, requiring a case number and report for public record.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised license plate readers like Flock cameras after they aided in a homicide arrest last month. Flowers said a murderer was put behind bars and taken off the streets because of the Flock system. Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder said legislation, not removal, is the right path forward and called for meaningful legislation that regulates camera use, protects privacy, but allows agencies to keep the cameras and keep the community safe.

Stuart resident Sean Reilly said he has never supported the cameras and thinks they are an invasion of privacy. Stuart resident Brandee Bailey said license plate readers play an important role in keeping the community safe and called the technology super important to catch the bad guys. Stuart resident Kristina Ramsey said the cameras have definitely helped catch a lot of criminals.

Budensiek said the cameras helped arrest President Donald Trump's would-be assassin, stopped a kidnapper with two young girls headed to Nebraska, and caught a traveling rooftop burglary crew. Flowers praised the license plate readers after they aided in a homicide arrest last month. Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder called for meaningful legislation that regulates camera use and protects privacy rather than removal, saying without cameras on US-1 it's a needle in a haystack.

Stuart resident Sean Reilly said he has never supported the cameras and called them an invasion of privacy. Neighbor Brandee Bailey said license plate readers play an important role in keeping the community safe and catching bad guys. Neighbor Kristina Ramsey said the cameras have helped catch a lot of criminals.

Budensiek proposed limiting camera use to criminal investigations and missing persons cases, requiring a case number and report for public record. Budensiek said he would be OK with a public professional auditing system if people still don't trust law enforcement.

hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office discovered a body in the mangroves on Hutchinson Island on Tuesday that investigators believe belongs to Michael Anthony Debevec II, an Oklahoma visitor who was reported missing after being last seen at Chastain Beach on August 26. The body was found just north of the House of Refuge heavily decomposed, and the clothing matched what Debevec was last seen wearing in surveillance video.

Debevec's family filed a missing person report on Saturday after a good Samaritan found his wallet on the beach near the House of Refuge and attempted to return it by going to his home. Deputies discovered Debevec's car parked at Chastain Beach, just down the road from where the body was found. The Martin County Sheriff's Office searched the area of Hutchinson Island by land, sea and air.

On Tuesday morning, investigators found Debevec's backpack hanging high in a tree half a mile south of the House of Refuge with a computer inside. As they continued through the thick mangroves and sea grapes, they located the deceased body. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the family told investigators Debevec has gone missing before and has a history of substance abuse, but had gotten clean.

The Medical Examiner's Office is working to determine the exact cause of death, looking for signs of trauma and performing a toxicology report. Investigators are waiting for a positive identification, though Budensiek said he believes the body belongs to Debevec based on the matching clothing.
